items.label: f04-type-defaults
items.front: nopCommerce schema defaults when a builder says nothing
items.back: string -> AsString(int.MaxValue).Nullable(), decimal -> decimal(18,4), DateTime -> provider datetime2; an Id identity key is added; ForeignKey<T> defaults to onDelete Rule.Cascade.

items.label: f01-three-questions
items.front: The three reliability questions to ask of any side effect
items.back: What if it fails? What if it runs twice? How would we know? Then match the reliability budget to the cost of loss: in nopCommerce only queued email is durable and retried (max 3 tries).

items.label: f03-repository-semantics
items.back: InsertAsync(list), DeleteAsync(list) and DeleteAsync(predicate) use CreateTransactionScope. Single-entity Insert/Update/Delete are single statements. UpdateAsync(list) is NOT atomic: a loop of single updates. There is no unit of work.

items.label: f02-login-gates
items.back: CAPTCHA -> validator -> phone branch -> lookup (CustomerNotExist) -> Deleted / NotActive / NotRegistered -> lockout window (before the password) -> password (count, maybe lock, WrongPassword) -> MFA required? -> success bookkeeping -> sign-in (migrate guest cart).

items.prompt: An hourly task runs for 10 minutes on node A. Its lock key expires, node B starts the task and sets the key again, and then A finishes first. What does A's finally block do?

choices.text: It throws, because the key now holds a different owner value
It extends B's lock by another 299 seconds before returning
It leaves the key alone, since A no longer owns the lock
It removes the key, so the lock of node B goes with it

choices: It throws, because the key now holds a different owner value
It extends B's lock by another 299 seconds before returning
It leaves the key alone, since A no longer owns the lock
It removes the key, so the lock of node B goes with it

items.explanation: The finally calls RemoveAsync(resource) unconditionally, with no owner token check, so a slow first runner deletes the second runner's key. The key lifetime is min(Seconds, 300) - 1 = 299 s for an hourly task.

items.prompt: An event type implements IStopProcessingEvent. Of four registered consumers, the second handles the event and sets StopProcessing = true without throwing. What happens to consumers three and four?

choices.text: They still run; the flag just marks the event as handled
They do not run, since the loop breaks after the second
They are skipped if the second consumer also threw
They run, but the publisher discards whatever they changed

choices: They still run; the flag just marks the event as handled
They do not run, since the loop breaks after the second
They are skipped if the second consumer also threw
They run, but the publisher discards whatever they changed

items.explanation: After each successful HandleEventAsync, PublishAsync checks @event is IStopProcessingEvent { StopProcessing: true } and breaks out of the foreach, so later consumers never run. The check sits inside the try after the await, so it applies to a consumer that completed normally.

items.prompt: A customer's add-to-cart is rejected for being out of stock. What happened to their selected shipping and payment choices?

choices.text: They were copied to a backup and restored after the warning
They were kept, since a rejected add has no side effects
They were cleared only if the cart then became empty
They were cleared, because ResetCheckoutDataAsync ran first

choices: They were copied to a backup and restored after the warning
They were kept, since a rejected add has no side effects
They were cleared only if the cart then became empty
They were cleared, because ResetCheckoutDataAsync ran first

items.explanation: AddToCartAsync calls ResetCheckoutDataAsync(customer, storeId) before any item warnings are computed, so a rejected add still wipes shipping option, pickup point, payment method and reward-points choice.

items.prompt: A product was soft-deleted (Deleted = true). Code calls the repository's GetByIdAsync(productId, includeDeleted: false) with no cache key. What comes back?

choices.text: The product, but with its Deleted flag reset to false
A NotFoundException for the filtered entity
The product, since a single-id lookup skips filters
null, because the deleted filter drops that row

choices: The product, but with its Deleted flag reset to false
A NotFoundException for the filtered entity
The product, since a single-id lookup skips filters
null, because the deleted filter drops that row

items.explanation: With includeDeleted false, AddDeletedFilter adds Where(!Deleted) for an ISoftDeletedEntity such as Product, and FirstOrDefaultAsync over the filtered query returns null. The default is includeDeleted = true, which is why callers must ask for the filter explicitly.

items.prompt: Two web nodes run the same scheduled task at the same moment. Both call DistributedCacheLocker.PerformActionWithLockAsync. What can happen?

choices.text: Only one runs, since Redis serializes the whole method call
Only one runs: SetStringAsync fails if the key already exists
Both may run the task, as the get and the set are separate calls
Neither runs, because each sees the other node's lock key

choices: Only one runs, since Redis serializes the whole method call
Only one runs: SetStringAsync fails if the key already exists
Both may run the task, as the get and the set are separate calls
Neither runs, because each sees the other node's lock key

items.explanation: The method reads the key with GetStringAsync and returns only if it is non-empty, then sets it with SetStringAsync. Nothing makes check-then-set atomic, so both nodes can see it absent and both run the action.

items.prompt: Lockout was off and a customer built up FailedLoginAttempts = 7. An admin now sets FailedPasswordAllowedAttempts to 5. What happens on the customer's next wrong password?

choices.text: They are locked out only after reaching 12, i.e. 7 plus 5
Locked out at once, as the count of 8 already meets 5
They get 5 more tries, counted from the moment of the change
Nothing yet: the count restarts at 0 when the setting changes

choices: They are locked out only after reaching 12, i.e. 7 plus 5
Locked out at once, as the count of 8 already meets 5
They get 5 more tries, counted from the moment of the change
Nothing yet: the count restarts at 0 when the setting changes

items.explanation: The wrong-password branch increments the stored counter to 8 and locks when it is >= the allowed attempts, then resets the counter to 0. Nothing resets the counter when the setting changes.

items.prompt: FailedPasswordAllowedAttempts is set to 3 and a customer has 2 failed attempts recorded. They enter a wrong password a third time. What does ValidateCustomerAsync return for this attempt?

choices.text: WrongPassword, and the lock starts on the fourth
LockedOut, as the third failure reaches the limit
NotActive, as the account is disabled at the limit
WrongPassword, while it starts the lockout window

choices: WrongPassword, and the lock starts on the fourth
LockedOut, as the third failure reaches the limit
NotActive, as the account is disabled at the limit
WrongPassword, while it starts the lockout window

items.explanation: The wrong-password branch increments the counter to 3, sees 3 >= 3, sets CannotLoginUntilDateUtc and resets the counter, then returns WrongPassword. LockedOut comes from the earlier gate, so it is returned on the next attempt inside the window.

items.prompt: Inside EventPublisher's catch block, suppose resolving ILogger returned null while handling the second of five consumers. What happens to consumers three to five?

choices.text: They are skipped, as the catch returns from the method
They are queued and run by the next scheduled task
They run after a retry of the second consumer succeeds
They still run; the null logger only loses the log entry

choices: They are skipped, as the catch returns from the method
They are queued and run by the next scheduled task
They run after a retry of the second consumer succeeds
They still run; the null logger only loses the log entry

items.explanation: The nested try does `if (logger == null) return;`, which exits PublishAsync entirely, so the foreach never reaches the remaining consumers. The guide calls it a latent edge.
